title: Gas Station — The Single-Pass Circular Greedy
summary: The single-pass greedy for the circular gas-station problem, and the reset rule — a compressed exchange argument — that makes one scan sufficient.

slides.markdown:
`n` gas stations sit in a circle, each giving some amount of gas and costing some amount to reach the next one. Find the single starting station (if one exists) from which you can complete the entire circular route without ever running out of gas.

The naive approach tries every station as a starting point and simulates the whole loop — O(n²). The greedy approach finds the answer in one O(n) pass, using a reset rule that's really a compressed version of the exchange argument this group has been building toward: if starting somewhere fails, an entire range of other starting points can be ruled out at once, for free.

A valid starting point exists **if and only if** total gas across all stations is >= total cost across all routes. This is worth checking (or computing as a byproduct) up front, because it's the fast, unconditional answer to "does a solution exist at all" — if this fails, no amount of clever starting-point selection can succeed, since the total gas physically isn't enough to cover the total distance no matter where you begin.

If total gas equals or exceeds total cost, a valid single starting point is **guaranteed to exist and be unique** — that guarantee is what the rest of this topic's algorithm relies on.

Scan stations left to right, maintaining a running tank balance starting from a candidate start. If the tank ever goes negative at station `j` (having started the candidate run at station `i`), then **no station between `i` and `j`, inclusive, could have worked as a starting point either** — try the next candidate starting right after `j`, and reset the running tank to zero.

Why skipping all of `i` through `j` is safe: any station `k` strictly between `i` and `j` starts with an empty tank (0), which is worse than or equal to whatever surplus the tank had built up by the time it reached `k` starting from `i`. If the tank still went negative by `j` even with that surplus, it would go negative at least as fast starting from `k`'s worse position. This is the exchange-argument-style reasoning that lets one failed attempt eliminate a whole contiguous block of candidates.

Picture a running total drawn as a line over the stations, starting at 0 for a candidate start. It dips and rises with each station's `gas - cost`. The moment it dips below 0, mark that point, reset the candidate start to the very next station, and restart the running total at 0 from there.

![Cumulative tank balance across eight stations, dipping below zero and resetting at station 4, then climbing to end above zero](assets/gas-station-tank-balance.svg)

The final candidate start standing after one full pass is the answer, provided the feasibility check from the previous slide passed.

assets.alt: Cumulative tank balance across eight stations, dipping below zero and resetting at station 4, then climbing to end above zero

slides.markdown:
```python
def can_complete_circuit(gas, cost):
    total_surplus, tank, start = 0, 0, 0
    for i in range(len(gas)):
        diff = gas[i] - cost[i]
        total_surplus += diff
        tank += diff
        if tank < 0:
            start = i + 1
            tank = 0
    return start if total_surplus >= 0 else -1
```

One pass computes both the feasibility check (`total_surplus`) and the candidate answer (`start`) simultaneously — no need for two separate loops. The final `start` is only meaningful (guaranteed correct) if `total_surplus >= 0`.

The naive approach — for each of the `n` candidate starting stations, simulate the entire loop from scratch to see if it succeeds — is O(n²), and it's the instinct most people reach for first because it's the most literal translation of the problem statement into code.

It's not wrong, just needlessly slow: it throws away the reset rule's insight that a single failed simulation already tells you about a whole range of other candidates, not just the one you tried. If you find yourself writing a nested loop for this problem, that's the signal to look for the O(n) single-pass structure instead — the reset rule is exactly the piece of information the O(n²) approach is failing to reuse.

slides.sectionTitle: The reset as a compressed exchange argument
slides.markdown:
The reset rule is doing exactly what an exchange argument does — showing that a whole set of alternative choices (every candidate start between `i` and `j`) can be ruled out without individually testing each one, because each is provably no better than the one that already failed.

The difference from the `exchange-argument` topic's presentation is compression: instead of a one-at-a-time swap-and-induct argument, gas station's reasoning eliminates an entire contiguous range in one step. This is worth recognizing explicitly as the same underlying technique wearing a faster-acting form — a good reminder that the general template doesn't always show up as a slow, step-by-step induction; sometimes the structure of the problem lets it fire in bulk.

| | Jump Game | Gas Station |
|---|---|---|
| Running quantity | Furthest reachable index — only ever grows | Tank balance — can go negative, triggering a reset |
| On failure | Entire problem fails (index unreachable) | Only the current candidate fails; scan continues from a new one |
| Shape | Linear, one direction | Circular, wraps around |

Both track a single running budget in one linear pass, which is why they read as similar at a glance — but Jump Game's budget only grows and failure is terminal, while Gas Station's budget can reset and failure only eliminates a range of candidates, not the whole search. Recognizing the difference (does the running quantity ever legitimately reset, or does failure end everything?) is a useful quick check when a new problem reminds you of one but not the other.

slides.sectionTitle: Why the valid start is unique
slides.markdown:
When `total_surplus >= 0`, exactly one valid starting station exists (assuming the problem's usual framing where all gas/cost values are such that ties don't produce multiple equally-valid answers). Two different valid starts would each need to independently survive the full loop without going negative — but the reset rule's logic implies that once a station survives from some start, every station *between* an earlier failed attempt and that surviving one was already provably excluded.

This uniqueness is part of why the single-pass approach can commit to one answer without any ambiguity about which of several valid starts to report — the problem structure itself only leaves room for one.

The single-pass version above avoids circular indexing entirely by construction — it never needs to wrap the index back to 0, because the reset logic guarantees the final `start` value, scanned linearly through to the end of the array, is already correct without a second wraparound pass.

A common but unnecessary complication: writing code that explicitly simulates the circular wraparound (using modulo arithmetic to loop back to index 0) when verifying the found answer. This isn't wrong, but it's extra complexity the core algorithm doesn't need — the reset-based single pass proves correctness through the array's natural linear order alone, precisely because of the total-surplus feasibility guarantee from earlier in this topic. If you find yourself reaching for modulo arithmetic here, double-check whether it's actually load-bearing or just an unnecessary reflex from the problem's circular framing.

O(n) time, O(1) space — one pass, three running variables (`total_surplus`, `tank`, `start`). This is the payoff of recognizing the reset rule's compressed-exchange-argument structure: it turns an apparently O(n²) problem (test every start) into a single linear scan, with no table and no revisiting of any station once passed.
